This character buys the record "Little Shirley Beans" for his sister, before breaking it after leaving the Wicker Bar at the Seton Hotel. Name this 17th century playwright of The Imaginary Invalid, The Misanthrope, Tartuffe, and The Miser.

At one point in this work one character claims that she was born when her mother plucked her from a rose bush. Name this Englishman who penned "Terence, this is stupid stuff," "To an Athlete Dying Young," and "When I was one-and-twenty."

Passages from the work include the lines, "Rejoice with me; I have found my lost sheep," and "Do not be afraid. I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people." Unlike her son Ronny Heaslop, in this novel Mrs. Moore is interested in the culture of the non-European residents of Chandrapore. He wasn't Swiss, but his name is a corruption of the German. He escapes from Moorish captors with the company of Xury and makes his way to Brazil where he starts a plantation. He set the Joan of Arc story in 1920s Chicago, depicting "Joan Dark's" struggles with an evil meat packing tycoon in Saint Joan of the Stockyards, and many of his works encouraged audience judgments and showcased workers' rights in what he called "Epic Theater." Works by this author, like The Making of Americans: The Hersland Family and Brewsie and Willie, are largely unknown. Born in 1612 in Northampton, England she would not immigrate to Massachusetts until she was already married to a future governor of that Colony. The ruler of the tiny oppressed island nation San Lorenzo offers a job to the son of an atomic scientist, and while there he learns about karasses, wampeters, and granfalloons, all parts of the banned religion of Bokonism, and the ritual of touching bare feet called Boku-Maru is a capital offense. In 2005's The Mysterious Flame of Queen Loana, an amnesiac rare books dealer discovers a copy of Shakespeare's first folio while trying to remember his role in the second World War. The publication of his most famous work lead to his falling out with Charles Fox, which he tried to rectify in his Appeal from the New to the Old Whigs, and Immanuel Kant praised this man's Enquiry into the Origin of Our Ideas of the Sublime and Beautiful. This character has a wife alternatively named Teresa and Juana Guttiérez, though the author prefers the former name in the second part of the book. His autobiography is entitled Journey Continued, and he collaborated with Krishna Shah on For Your Departed. His most famous novel was made into the musical Lost in the Stars by Maxwell Anderson. Cold descending squalls known as elvegusts are prevalent around them, as are sikussaks, which are chunks of old sea ice that become trapped in them. He fictionalized his time spent in Spain in the work Rosinante to the Road Again. His philosophical writings can be found in Aids to Reflection, and he dabbled in drama, collaborating with Robert Southey to write The Fall of Robespierre and focusing on the titular emotion in Remorse. He lives in a mansion in Fauborg St. Germain with a rich young man he met in a bookstore. Identify this detective who solved "The Mystery of Marie Roget," "The Purloined Letter" and "The Murders in the Rue Morgue."
